title: India Did Not Qualify for the World Cup. Four Players of Indian Origin Will Be There Anyway.
excerpt: From Auckland to Doha, from Melbourne to Guadeloupe — four footballers with roots in Punjab, Kerala, and Tamil Nadu will represent New Zealand, Australia, Qatar, and DR Congo at the 2026 FIFA World Cup.
body:
India has never played at a senior men's FIFA World Cup. In 1950, they qualified but withdrew, citing travel costs and a preference for the 1952 Olympics. Seventy-six years later, the national team still watches from outside. But starting Wednesday, when the 2026 FIFA World Cup kicks off in Mexico City, four men of Indian heritage will be on the pitch.

It is a small number. It is also historic. Never before have four players with Indian roots featured in the same World Cup.

## Sarpreet Singh — New Zealand

Sarpreet Singh was born in Auckland to Punjabi parents. He is 27, left-footed, plays as an attacking midfielder, and wears the number 10 shirt for New Zealand's All Whites.

Singh's football education took him to Bayern Munich's reserve team in Germany before he returned to the A-League with Wellington Phoenix, where he currently plays. His creative passing and smart movement during qualifying locked in his place in Darren Bazeley's 26-man squad.

New Zealand are in Group G alongside Belgium, Egypt, and Iran. Their first match is against Iran on June 15 at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles. For Indian-origin fans on the American West Coast, it will be the closest thing to cheering for one of their own at a World Cup.

## Nishan Velupillay — Australia

Nishan Velupillay was born in Melbourne to an Anglo-Indian mother and a Tamil father. He plays as a forward and winger, and earned his spot in the Socceroos squad after a breakout season under coach Tony Popovic.

His debut was unforgettable: Velupillay scored against China in his first senior international during the qualifiers. He is exactly the kind of explosive, counter-attacking threat Australia need in a group that includes the United States, Paraguay, and Turkey.

Australia open their campaign against the US on June 12 at SoFi Stadium. Velupillay's pace on the wing could make him one of the stories of the group stage.

## Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid — Qatar

At 19, Tahsin Mohammed Jamshid is the youngest of the four — and the one with the most direct Indian connection. He was born in Doha to Malayali parents from Kannur, Kerala. His father Jamshid played football for the University of Calicut before moving to Qatar in 1996 as an accountant.

Tahsin trained at Qatar's Aspire Academy before joining Al Duhail, where he emerged as one of the country's most exciting young wingers. He made his senior debut in a World Cup qualifier against Afghanistan in June 2024. He holds an Indian passport, making him the first Indian passport holder selected for a World Cup squad.

Qatar face Switzerland on June 13 at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara — right in the Bay Area. For the Malayali diaspora in Silicon Valley, it doesn't get more personal than this.

## Samuel Moutoussamy — DR Congo

Samuel Moutoussamy's connection to India runs through his father, who comes from a South Indian Tamil family in Guadeloupe, the French Caribbean territory. Born in France, Moutoussamy is a central midfielder whose composure and work rate made him indispensable during DR Congo's African qualifiers.

He plays club football in Europe and brings precisely the kind of experience and consistency that DR Congo need in Group K, where they face Portugal, Uzbekistan, and Colombia.

## Why it matters for the diaspora

India has 18 million people in its overseas diaspora. The World Cup has always been something NRIs watched as neutrals or adopted fans. This time, there are players to claim.

A Punjabi midfielder in New Zealand. A Tamil winger in Australia. A Malayali teenager in Qatar. A Tamil-origin midfielder in DR Congo. They play for different flags, speak different languages, and grew up in different football cultures. But for the Indian diaspora scattered across the world, they represent something that has been absent from the global stage: proof that Indian-origin talent belongs at the highest level of the world's most popular sport.

The 2026 World Cup runs from June 11 to July 19 across 16 stadiums in the US, Canada, and Mexico.

*Sources: Jagran Josh, Livemint, Reuters, Football365*
